title: Handles and Kernel Objects
summary: Files, threads, processes, events and many other resources are **kernel objects**: they live inside the Windows kernel, and your program refers to them only through **handles**. This lesson explains what a handle is, the rules for getting and closing one, the two different "invalid" values, and how to wrap handles in an RAII class so they can never leak.
markdown:
## Objects you cannot touch When a program opens a file, Windows creates a **file object** inside the kernel: a structure recording which file, the current position, the access rights granted, and more. That structure lives in kernel memory, which user-mode code cannot read (lesson 1.06). So instead of a pointer, the program gets a **handle**, a small number that identifies the object within this process. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph P["Your process"] H["HANDLE h = 0x1A4"] end subgraph K["Kernel"] T["Handle table of your process
0x1A4 → file object, rights: read"] O["File object
C:\save\slot1.dat, position 0"] end H --> T --> O ``` Every process has its own **handle table**. A handle value means nothing outside its process, just like a virtual address. When you pass the handle back to Windows, for example to `ReadFile`, the kernel looks it up in your table, checks the rights recorded there, and acts on the object. Many kinds of object work this way: | Object | Created by | Used for | |---|---|---| | File | `CreateFileW` | Reading and writing files, pipes, devices | | Thread | `CreateThread` | Running code in parallel (chapter 6) | | Process | `CreateProcessW`, `OpenProcess` | Starting programs, waiting for them (chapter 6) | | Event, mutex, semaphore | `CreateEventW`, `CreateMutexW`, ... | Synchronising threads (chapter 6) | | File mapping | `CreateFileMappingW` | Shared memory between processes (chapter 12) | Windows also has **window handles** (`HWND`), **GDI handles** (`HBRUSH`, `HDC`) and **module handles** (`HMODULE`). They look similar but are managed by different parts of Windows and closed with different functions. This lesson is about kernel object handles, closed with `CloseHandle`. ## Getting and closing a handle ```cpp #include #include int main() { HANDLE ready{ CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, FALSE, nullptr) }; // a manual-reset event, not yet signalled if (ready == nullptr) { std::cout << "CreateEventW failed: " << GetLastError() << '\n'; return 1; } SetEvent(ready); // signal it const DWORD result{ WaitForSingleObject(ready, 0) }; // is it signalled? (don't wait) std::cout << (result == WAIT_OBJECT_0 ? "the event is signalled" : "not signalled") << '\n'; CloseHandle(ready); // give the handle back return 0; } ``` ``` the event is signalled ``` The rules: 1. **Every handle you open, you must close**, exactly once, with the matching function. Kernel objects are reference-counted: the object is destroyed when its last handle is closed. 2. **After closing, the value is meaningless.** Windows reuses handle values, so a stale handle can end up referring to a different object, just like a dangling pointer (lesson 2.09). 3. **When the process ends, Windows closes everything it left open.** That is a safety net, not a plan: a game that leaks a handle per frame runs out within hours. Task Manager can show leaks: on the **Details** tab, right-click the column headers → **Select columns** → **Handles**. A number that keeps growing while the game runs is a handle leak. ## Two kinds of "invalid" A historical wart: failing functions do not all return the same value. | Function | Returns on failure | |---|---| | `CreateFileW` | `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE` (which is `-1`) | | `CreateEventW`, `CreateThread`, `OpenProcess`, most others | `nullptr` (0) | The documentation for each function says which. Checking for the wrong one is a classic bug: `if (h == nullptr)` after `CreateFileW` never catches a failure. ## An RAII wrapper Lesson 2.04's RAII idea is a perfect fit. A small class owns the handle and closes it in its destructor: ```cpp #include #include #include class UniqueHandle { public: UniqueHandle() = default; explicit UniqueHandle(HANDLE h) : m_handle{ h } {} ~UniqueHandle() { reset(); } UniqueHandle(const UniqueHandle&) = delete; // one owner only UniqueHandle& operator=(const UniqueHandle&) = delete; UniqueHandle(UniqueHandle&& other) noexcept : m_handle{ std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr) } {} UniqueHandle& operator=(UniqueHandle&& other) noexcept { if (this != &other) { reset(); m_handle = std::exchange(other.m_handle, nullptr); } return *this; } HANDLE get() const { return m_handle; } explicit operator bool() const { return m_handle != nullptr && m_handle != INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE; } void reset() { if (*this) CloseHandle(m_handle); m_handle = nullptr; } private: HANDLE m_handle{ nullptr }; }; int main() { UniqueHandle event{ CreateEventW(nullptr, TRUE, TRUE, nullptr) }; if (!event) return 1; std::cout << (WaitForSingleObject(event.get(), 0) == WAIT_OBJECT_0) << '\n'; return 0; } // closed here, on every path out of main ``` ``` 1 ``` Treating both `nullptr` and `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE` as "no handle" makes the class safe whichever function produced the value. The Windows Implementation Libraries (WIL, available through vcpkg as `wil`) provide polished versions of this for every handle type: `wil::unique_handle`, `wil::unique_hfile`, `wil::unique_event`. ## Common mistakes > [!warning] Checking `CreateFileW`'s result against `nullptr` > It returns `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE` on failure. Read each function's documentation. > [!warning] Closing a handle twice > The second `CloseHandle` may close an unrelated object that reused the value. Under a debugger, Windows raises an "invalid handle" exception for it. > [!warning] Closing a window, module or GDI handle with `CloseHandle` > They have their own functions: `DestroyWindow`, `FreeLibrary`, `DeleteObject`, `ReleaseDC`. > [!warning] Copying a raw handle into two owners > Only one should close it. If two parts of the program genuinely need their own handle, use `DuplicateHandle`. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? Why does Windows give programs handles instead of pointers to kernel objects? - Handles are smaller than pointers and save memory + Kernel memory is off-limits; a handle lets the kernel check each use - Pointers would change every time the program restarted - Handles can be shared with other computers over a network > A pointer into kernel memory would be useless to user-mode code, and it would skip the kernel's permission check. ? What happens to a process's open handles when it exits? + Windows closes them all, and any object whose last handle that was is destroyed - They stay open until the computer restarts - They are passed on to the parent process - They become invalid but the objects leak until someone closes them > Leaked handles are still a bug while the program runs, but they do not outlive the process. ? Why does the `UniqueHandle` class treat both `nullptr` and `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE` as empty? - Because they are the same value on 64-bit Windows - Because `CloseHandle` crashes on any other value - Because `nullptr` means "not opened yet" and the other means "already closed" + Because different Windows functions use different values to mean failure > `CreateFileW` fails with `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE`, many others with null, so checking both makes the class safe whatever produced the handle. ? What is a handle? + A per-process number naming a kernel object it opened - A pointer to the kernel object's memory - A global id shared by every process > The object lives in kernel memory; the handle is how your process names it. ? What does `CreateFileW` return when it fails? - `nullptr` + `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE` - 0 or -1, at random > Most other creation functions return `nullptr`; `CreateFileW` is one of the exceptions. ? A kernel object has two open handles. One is closed. What happens to the object? - It is destroyed immediately - The other handle becomes invalid + Nothing yet: it goes when its last handle closes > Kernel objects are reference-counted. ? Why wrap handles in an RAII class? + So they are closed exactly once, automatically, on every path out of the scope - Because raw handles cannot be passed to Windows functions - To make them faster > The destructor guarantees `CloseHandle` runs, even on early returns and exceptions. ```
ideas:
- Run the event example in Visual Studio with a breakpoint before `CloseHandle`, and look at the handle's value in the Watch window.
- Write a loop that creates 10,000 events without closing them, and watch the program's handle count in Task Manager. Then use `UniqueHandle` and watch it stay flat.
- Install WIL with vcpkg and replace `UniqueHandle` with `wil::unique_event`.

cards.q: Why does Windows give programs handles instead of pointers to kernel objects?
cards.a:
Kernel memory is off-limits; a handle lets the kernel check each use

A pointer into kernel memory would be useless to user-mode code, and it would skip the kernel's permission check.

cards.q: What happens to a process's open handles when it exits?
cards.a:
Windows closes them all, and any object whose last handle that was is destroyed

Leaked handles are still a bug while the program runs, but they do not outlive the process.

cards.q: Why does the `UniqueHandle` class treat both `nullptr` and `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE` as empty?
cards.a:
Because different Windows functions use different values to mean failure

`CreateFileW` fails with `INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE`, many others with null, so checking both makes the class safe whatever produced the handle.

A per-process number naming a kernel object it opened

The object lives in kernel memory; the handle is how your process names it.

cards.q: What does `CreateFileW` return when it fails?
cards.a:
`INVALID_HANDLE_VALUE`

Most other creation functions return `nullptr`; `CreateFileW` is one of the exceptions.

cards.q: A kernel object has two open handles. One is closed. What happens to the object?
cards.a:
Nothing yet: it goes when its last handle closes

Kernel objects are reference-counted.

cards.q: Why wrap handles in an RAII class?
cards.a:
So they are closed exactly once, automatically, on every path out of the scope

The destructor guarantees `CloseHandle` runs, even on early returns and exceptions.
